summary: Presents objectives for an interoperable protocol for the Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points. It aims to set focused requirements for developing and evaluating such a protocol, covering architecture, operation, security and network operator needs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A big building has many Wi-Fi boxes. This lists what a single protocol should do so one controller can set up and manage all of them, whoever made them.

questions: what is a wireless termination point
subtitle: The wish list for a protocol that lets one controller configure and manage many wireless access points from different makers.

tldr.problem: Large wireless LAN deployments are hard to manage. Many Wireless Termination Points (WTPs) must be kept consistent, the wireless medium is dynamic, security is a worry, and vendor designs differ.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists objectives a CAPWAP protocol must meet, ranked as Mandatory and Accepted, Desirable, or Non-Objectives, plus one operator requirement. They cover architecture, operations and security.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a protocol. It was meant to be used with the CAPWAP Problem Statement and Architecture Taxonomy to develop and evaluate a protocol.

today: RFC 4564 is an Informational document from July 2006. According to the unit metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements for a protocol rather than defining one.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
Large-scale wireless LAN (WLAN) deployments are hard to manage. There are many Wireless Termination Points (WTPs) with varied designs, they need consistent configuration, the wireless medium is dynamic, and security matters. These challenges are described in RFC 3990. The Architecture Taxonomy in RFC 4118 classifies WLAN architectures as autonomous, centralized WLAN and distributed mesh.

In the centralized architecture, part of the wireless MAC is run in a WLAN controller. It is further split into remote-MAC, split-MAC and local-MAC designs. The CAPWAP framework covers local-MAC and split-MAC. The CAPWAP protocol is the one between the WLAN controller and WTPs. A logical group is a logical slice of a physical WTP, such as a virtual access point identified by a BSSID.
sections.plainLanguage: Many Wi-Fi boxes are hard to look after one by one. The aim is a common language so one controller can look after all of them, even if different companies made them.

sections.title: How Objectives Are Ranked
sections.content:
The objectives are grouped by classification into architecture, operations, security and general. They are also prioritized by working group discussion. Mandatory and Accepted objectives are crucial and MUST be realized by a CAPWAP protocol. Desirable objectives may help but are not required for all networks. Non-Objectives were consciously ruled out for CAPWAP. A separate category holds Operator Requirements gathered from network service operators.

Each objective is written in the same pattern: description, protocol requirement, motivation and benefits, and its relation to the Problem Statement.
sections.plainLanguage: Some items on the list are must-haves, some are nice-to-haves, and some are things the group decided not to do.

sections.title: Mandatory Architecture and Operations Objectives
sections.content:
Mandatory objectives include:

  • Logical groups: the protocol MUST manage physical WTPs in terms of logical groups, including BSSID-based groups.
  • Traffic separation: control messages MUST be transported separately from data messages.
  • Wireless terminal transparency: wireless terminals MUST NOT be required to know about CAPWAP.
  • Configuration consistency: WTPs and the controller MUST exchange state information regularly, such as processing load and memory use.
  • Firmware trigger: the protocol MUST support a trigger for firmware updates, though delivery itself need not be part of it.
  • Resource state and control: it MUST allow exchange of statistics and congestion information, and MUST map IEEE 802.11e QoS priorities across the switching and wireless medium segments.
sections.plainLanguage: The must-haves are things like treating each virtual Wi-Fi network separately, keeping control messages apart from your data, and not asking phones or laptops to change anything.

sections.title: Interoperability and General Objectives
sections.content:
The interoperability objective says WTPs of both local-MAC and split-MAC designs must work within a single WLAN under one CAPWAP protocol. The protocol MUST include enough capability negotiation to tell the major WTP types apart. It also has to handle IEEE 802.11i cases where the authenticator (at the controller) and the encryption points (at the WTPs) are on distinct entities, so it MUST allow exchange of key information in that case.

General mandatory objectives say anyone MUST be able to implement the protocol from the specification and have implementations interoperate. A WTP vendor SHOULD be able to change hardware without controller vendor involvement. The protocol MUST NOT limit vendors to local-MAC or split-MAC and MUST NOT prevent established NAT traversal methods.
sections.plainLanguage: Boxes built in different ways must still be able to talk to the same boss computer, and anyone should be able to build one just by reading the rules.

sections.title: Security Objectives and Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol MUST support mutual authentication of WTPs and the controller, so rogue WTPs and rogue controllers are kept out. Session keys MUST be derived using entropy from both parties. Exchanges MUST be integrity protected, replay protection is required, and confidentiality through encryption is a SHOULD. If the protocol meets the criteria for automated key management in BCP 107 (RFC 4107), mutual authentication MUST use an authenticated key exchange. The design MUST NOT allow compromises of the WLAN by external entities, and a single breached WTP should not affect the whole WLAN.

The Security Considerations section adds that logical-group traffic must stay separated, that sharing the 802.11i Pairwise Master Key across WTPs raises an ambiguity between legitimate sharing and illegitimate copies, and that non-mutual (asymmetric) authentication is best avoided except where legitimacy is verified externally, for example by physical containment.
sections.plainLanguage: The boss computer and each Wi-Fi box must prove who they are to each other, and one stolen box must not let a thief into the whole network.

sections.title: Desirable Objectives, Non-Objectives and Operator Needs
sections.content:
Desirable objectives include supporting authentication mechanisms beyond IEEE 802.11i, being extensible to other layer 2 wireless technologies such as IEEE 802.16, absorbing new IEEE 802.11 definitions with minimal change, running over IPv4 and IPv6 and different interconnections, and carrying access control information for WTPs and wireless terminals.

Two items were ranked as non-objectives: recognizing non-CAPWAP (legacy) WTPs, and not requiring vendors to share technical specifications, which was judged a duplicate of the Protocol Specifications objective. The one operator requirement is that CAPWAP operations MUST NOT impede AP fast-handoff procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The nice-to-haves make the system flexible for the future. The operators only ask one thing: do not slow down moving between Wi-Fi boxes.
